body.text: The 31st climate talks (COP31) are under way in Antalya, Türkiye, where the joint Türkiye-Australia presidencies have touted a flagship global electrification pledge that seeks to increase the share of electricity in final energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035 (35x35).

The target draws on analyses by the International Renewable Energy Agency and the International Energy Agency (IEA). The pledge has the support of a handful of countries such as Pakistan, Germany, Norway, and Ethiopia, which is set to host COP32 next year.

India has expressed reservations about the pledge on grounds of equity. A target based on the share of electricity can be met by expanding electricity use or by holding down total energy use. The IEA’s own scenarios note that, reducing total final energy consumption, the denominator of the electrification rate, therefore contributes to increasing the overall electrification rate. For countries such as India, where energy use per person is still well below the global average, meeting a uniform 35 per cent target could mean constraining the energy growth needed for development.

At present, electricity accounts for around 18 per cent of India’s final energy consumption. Globally, its share rose from 17 per cent in 2000 to 23 per cent in 2025. Reaching 35 per cent by 2035 requires five times that annual pace.

Ankita Ranjan, a research associate at the National Institute of Advanced Studies, Bengaluru, told Frontline: “Electrification matters for development, but a 35 per cent share tells you nothing about whether people have enough energy.” She added, “People need more energy, not a better ratio. Without equity, a single global number only shifts the burden onto those who did least to cause the problem.”

At a media huddle on November 13, Ajay Mathur, lead Indian negotiator 2006–12, India’s spokesperson in Paris, now professor of practice at IIT Delhi, said one of the challenges for developing countries, including India, is “the shift to the demand side”. It does not matter how much renewable energy capacity is added unless transport, industry, and cooking also move away from fossil fuels and towards electrification, he said, and that requires subsidies on both the supply and the demand side. Raising India’s electrification rate by 2035 was “certainly possible”, Mathur said, but “one global target applied equally to every country will be hard, because countries are starting from very different positions”.

The African Group of Negotiators (AGN) has also expressed concerns about the pledge. In an interview with this reporter for the magazine African Arguments, Nana Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, the chair of AGN, noted that, for the continent as a whole, energy access is the primary goal, with clean energy within it. The chair also cited a lack of clarity about baselines and other conditions associated with the 35x35 global target.
Electricity use in sub-Saharan Africa is about 200 kWh a person a year, whereas in advanced economies the figure is about 7,000 kWh.

“We want electricity generated from renewable sources, but electrification means something different in Africa than in developed countries,” said Dola Oluteye, a senior research fellow in energy and transport policy at University College London, during the media huddle. In parts of Europe, she said, it means replacing an existing fossil-fuelled system with a renewable one. “In Africa, the starting point is often no system at all: people are still relying on firewood, or have no electricity whatsoever, so this is not simply a question of substitution.” Affordability matters just as much, she added: once access is unlocked, the price of electricity has to compete with firewood, “which costs almost nothing to use”.
Unequal starting points

The story of electrification is also varied across developing countries. In India, renewable energy has grown rapidly, but the country still relies on coal to supply more than 70 per cent of its electricity demand. Pakistan has seen an organic adoption of solar panels at the household and small-business level, driven largely by the government's incapacity to deliver reliable round-the-clock grid power. But the “solar revolution” has also left poorer households behind on an even more expensive grid with fewer customers.

Ethiopia is having its moment in the sun, with household and community-level adoption of solar power. But overall, electricity access in Ethiopia is still only about 35 per cent. For Africa as a whole, too, access to energy remains a major issue, with firewood widely used for cooking at a high health cost. In some parts of rural India, too, the use of biomass for cooking is not uncommon.

The cost of capital matters too. According to the IEA, the cost of capital for utility-scale solar photovoltaic projects in emerging markets and developing economies is more than twice as high as in advanced economies.

China, on the other hand, has not signalled active enthusiasm for the pledge but has not opposed it either. At present, electricity accounts for close to 30 per cent of China’s final energy consumption, which puts the target well within reach.

Li Shuo, director of the China Climate Hub at the Asia Society Policy Institute, said during the media huddle that China might not be “a particularly active supporter” of the 35x35 target. “Its view is that COPs should focus on implementation, not on creating new targets,” he said. “That said, China is making considerable domestic progress, and reaching 35 per cent by 2035 would be a relatively easy target for it to hit.” Li added that, in the Chinese government’s view, plenty of targets have already been set in recent years, including mitigation goals such as tripling renewable capacity, doubling the rate of energy efficiency improvement and transitioning away from fossil fuels, many of which have not been fully implemented.
India’s options

According to an analysis by the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), India’s share of electricity in final energy could reach 27 per cent by 2035 on current trends, with a rapid build-out of clean power. Meeting the 35 per cent target would require additional efforts.

In another study, “Whose Transition? Unpacking the Discourse on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels in Climate Negotiations”, the think tank noted that, to ensure equity, some countries could take electrification rates of 40-45 per cent, allowing India a slower path so that the world still reaches 35 per cent. The study analysed 21 submissions to the COP30 presidency’s fossil fuel roadmap.

Nikit Abhyankar, a faculty member at the University of California, Berkeley, and co-faculty director of the India Energy and Climate Center, told Frontline that the 35x35 electrification pledge would be “very important” for India, given that electrification in transport and industry is needed for India’s energy security and industrial competitiveness and will create economic benefits.

During further negotiations, developing countries such as India are likely to seek differentiated pathways. On this, Abhyankar said it would be the right approach, as identical national percentages would be “a poor measure of comparable effort”. Industrialised economies have substantial space-heating demand and high car ownership, meaning large opportunities to replace fossil fuels with heat pumps and electric vehicles. Their relatively slow growth in overall energy consumption also makes it easier to increase electricity’s share.

On the other hand, emerging economies such as India face different conditions: much less space-heating demand, lower car ownership, and rapidly expanding energy needs as incomes and industrial production grow. “They must electrify while also meeting this additional demand,” he explained.

Abhyankar said, more broadly, India has strong economic and energy-security reasons to accelerate electrification in vehicles, cooking and industrial heat. “India’s priority should be building an affordable and reliable energy system, with minimal environmental impact, and commercially scalable business models, including access to low-cost financing,” he added.

It remains to be seen how the electrification pledge develops during negotiations in the second week of COP31. Neshwin Rodrigues, an energy analyst for Asia at the think tank Ember, said, “If India doesn’t sign, it won’t be because it opposes electrification. Higher electrification is already under way, and India’s own draft electricity policy expects electricity’s share of total energy use to double by 2047.”
Rishika Pardikar is an environment reporter based in Bengaluru who covers science, law, and policy.
